entries.95f124cdf32d0e40cddd35426e9daae6672e8b85: <div sID="gen16817" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="56" osisID="Isa.56" sID="Isa.56"/> <div eID="gen16817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16818" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16819" type="x-p"/> After the exceedingly great and precious promises of gospel grace, typified by temporal deliverances, which we had in the foregoing chapter, we have here, I. A solemn charge given to us all to make conscience of our duty, as we hope to have the benefit of those promises, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. Great encouragement given to strangers that were willing to come under the bonds of the covenant, assuring them of the blessings of the covenant, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3-Isa.56.8">ver. 3-8</reference>. III. A high charge drawn up against the watchmen of Israel, that were careless and unfaithful in the discharge of their duty (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.9-Isa.56.12">ver. 9-12</reference>), which seems to be the beginning of a new sermon, by way of reproof and threatening, which is continued in the following chapters. And the word of God was intended for conviction, as well as for comfort and instruction in righteousness.
entries.fb71baf7c9e65151eb0fd930609b6e0261df22f5: <div eID="gen16819" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16818" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Promises; Exhortations to Duty. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16820" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Keep ye judgment, and do justice: for my salvation <hi type="italic">is</hi> near to come, and my righteousness to be revealed. <hi type="super">2</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">is</hi> the man <hi type="italic">that</hi> doeth this, and the son of man <hi type="italic">that</hi> layeth hold on it; that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and keepeth his hand from doing any evil. <div eID="gen16820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16821" type="x-p"/> The scope of these verses is to show that when God is coming towards us in a way of mercy we must go forth to meet him in a way of duty. <div eID="gen16821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16822" type="x-p"/> I. God here tells us what are his intentions of mercy to us (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">My salvation is near to come</hi>—the great salvation wrought out by Jesus Christ (for that was the salvation of which the <hi type="italic">prophets enquired and searched diligently,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1 Pet. i. 10</reference>), typified by the salvation of the Jews from Sennacherib or out of Babylon. Observe, 1. The gospel salvation is the salvation of the Lord. It was contrived and brought about by him; he glories in it as his. 2. In that salvation God's righteousness is revealed, which is so much the beauty of the gospel that St. Paul makes this the ground of his glorying in it. (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.17">Rom. i. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">because therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith.</hi> The law revealed that righteousness of God by which all sinners stand condemned, but the gospel reveals that by which all believers stand acquitted. 3. The Old-Testament saints saw this salvation coming, and drawing near to them, long before it came; and they had notice by the prophets of its approach. As Daniel understood by Jeremiah's books the approach of the redemption out of Babylon, at the end of seventy years, so others understood by Daniel's books the approach of our redemption by Christ at the end of seventy weeks of years. <div eID="gen16822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16823" type="x-p"/> II. He tells us what are his expectations of duty from us, in consideration thereof. Say not, "We see the salvation near, and therefore we may live as we list, for there is no danger now of missing it or coming short of it;" that is turning the grace of God into wantonness. But, on the contrary, when the salvation is near double your guard against sin. Note, The fuller assurances God gives us of the performance of his promises the stronger obligations he lays us under to obedience. The salvation here spoken of has now come; yet, there being still a further salvation in view, the apostle presses duty upon us Christians with the same argument. <reference osisRef="Rom.3.11">Rom. iii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.</hi> That which is here required to qualify and prepare us for the approaching salvation is, <div eID="gen16823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16824" type="x-p"/> 1. That we be honest and just in all our dealings: <hi type="italic">Keep you judgment and do justice.</hi> Walk by rule, and make conscience of what you say and do, that you do no wrong to any. Render to all their dues exactly, and, in exacting what is due to you, keep up a court of equity in your own bosom, to moderate the rigours of the law. Be ruled by that golden rule, "Do as you would be done by." Magistrates must administer justice wisely and faithfully. This is required to evidence the sincerity of our faith and repentance, and to open the way of mercy. <hi type="italic">Repent for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> God is true to us; let us be so to one another. <div eID="gen16824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16825" type="x-p"/> 2. That we religiously observe the sabbath day, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.2">v. 2</reference>. We are not just if we rob God of his time. Sabbath-sanctification is here put for all the duties of the first table, the fruits of our love to God, as justice and judgment are put for all those of the second table, the fruits of our love to our neighbour. Observe, (1.) The duty required, which is to <hi type="italic">keep the sabbath,</hi> to keep it as a talent we are to trade with, as a treasure we are entrusted with. "Keep it holy; keep it safe; keep it with care and caution; keep it from polluting it. Allow neither yourselves nor others either to violate the holy rest or omit the holy work of that day." If this be intended primarily for the Jews in Babylon, it was fit that they should be particularly put in mind of this, because when, by reason of their distance from the temple, they could not observe the other institutions of their law, yet they might distinguish themselves from the heathen by putting a difference between God's day and other days. But it being required more generally of man, and <hi type="italic">the son of man,</hi> it intimates that sabbath-sanctification should be a duty in gospel times, when the bounds of the church should be enlarged and other rites and ceremonies abolished. Observe, Those that would keep the sabbath from polluting it must put on resolution, must not only do this, but lay hold on it, for sabbath time is precious, but is very apt to slip away if we take not great care; and therefore we must lay hold on it and keep our hold, must do it and persevere in it. (2.) The encouragement we have to do this duty: <hi type="italic">Blessed is he that doeth it.</hi> The way to have the blessing of God upon our employments all the week is to make conscience, and make a business, of sabbath-sanctification; and in doing so we shall be the better qualified to do judgment and justice. The more godliness the more honesty, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.2">1 Tim. ii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen16825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16826" type="x-p"/> 3. That we have nothing to do with sin: <hi type="italic">Blessed is the man</hi> that <hi type="italic">keeps his hand from doing evil,</hi> any wrong to his neighbour, in body, goods, or good name—or, more generally, any thing that is displeasing to God and hurtful to his own soul. Note, The best evidence of our having kept the sabbath well will be a care to keep a good conscience all the week. By this it will appear that we have been in the mount with God if our faces shine in a holy conversation before men.
entries.a41b3855230f542821303ec7a6f7cf6e748bd73a: <div eID="gen16826" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Encouragement to the Sincere; Encouragement to the Gentiles. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16827" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Neither let the son of the stranger, that hath joined himself to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , speak, saying, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath utterly separated me from his people: neither let the eunuch say, Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a dry tree. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto the eunuchs that keep my sabbaths, and choose <hi type="italic">the things</hi> that please me, and take hold of my covenant; <hi type="super">5</hi> Even unto them will I give in mine house and within my walls a place and a name better than of sons and of daughters: I will give them an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off. <hi type="super">6</hi> Also the sons of the stranger, that join themselves to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to serve him, and to love the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to be his servants, every one that keepeth the sabbath from polluting it, and taketh hold of my covenant; <hi type="super">7</hi> Even them will I bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer: their burnt offerings and their sacrifices <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> accepted upon mine altar; for mine house shall be called a house of prayer for all people. <hi type="super">8</hi> The Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> which gathereth the outcasts of Israel saith, Yet will I gather <hi type="italic">others</hi> to him, beside those that are gathered unto him. <div eID="gen16827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16828" type="x-p"/> The prophet is here, in God's name, encouraging those that were hearty in joining themselves to God and yet laboured under great discouragements. 1. Some were discouraged because they were not of the seed of Abraham. They had <hi type="italic">joined themselves to the Lord,</hi> and bound their souls with a bond to be his for ever (this is the root and life of religion, to break off from the world and the flesh, and devote ourselves entirely to the service and honour of God); but they questioned whether God would accept them, because they were of <hi type="italic">the sons of the stranger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">v. 3</reference>. They were Gentiles, strangers to the commonwealth of Israel and aliens from the covenants of promise, and therefore feared they had no part nor lot in the matter. They said, "<hi type="italic">The Lord has utterly separated me from his people,</hi> and will not own me as one of them, nor admit me to their privileges." It was often said that there should be <hi type="italic">one law for the stranger and for him that was born in the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.49">Exod. xii. 49</reference>), and yet they came to this melancholy conclusion. Note, Unbelief often suggests things to the discouragement of good people which are directly contrary to what God himself has said, things which he has expressly guarded against. Let not the <hi type="italic">sons of the stranger</hi> therefore say thus, for they have no reason to say it. Note, Ministers must have answers ready for the disquieting fears and jealousies of weak Christians, which, how unreasonable soever, they must take notice of. 2. Others were discouraged because they were not fathers in Israel. The eunuch said, <hi type="italic">Behold, I am a dry tree.</hi> So he looked upon himself, and it was his grief; so others looked upon him, and it was his reproach. He was thought to be of no use because he had no children, nor was ever likely to have any. This was then the more grievous because eunuchs were not admitted to be priests (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.20">Lev. xxi. 20</reference>), nor to <hi type="italic">enter into the congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.1">Deut. xxiii. 1</reference>), and because the promise of a numerous posterity was the particular blessing of Israel and the more valuable because from among them the Messiah was to come. Yet God would not have the eunuchs to make the worst of their case, nor to think that they should be excluded from the gospel church, and from being spiritual priests, because they were shut out from the congregation of Israel and the Levitical priesthood; no, as the taking down of the partition wall, contained in ordinances, admitted the Gentiles, so it let in likewise those that had been kept out by ceremonial pollutions. Yet, by the reply here given to this suggestion, it should seem the chief thing which the eunuch laments in his case is his being written childless. <div eID="gen16828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16829" type="x-p"/> Now suitable encouragements are given to each of these. <div eID="gen16829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16830" type="x-p"/> I. To those who have no children of their own, who, though they had the honour to be the children of the church and the covenant themselves, yet had none to whom they might transmit that honour, none to receive the sign of circumcision and the privileges secured by that sign. Now observe, <div eID="gen16830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16831" type="x-p"/> 1. What a good character they have, though they lie under this ignominy and affliction; and those only are entitled to the following comforts who in some measure answer to these characters. (1.) They <hi type="italic">keep God's sabbaths</hi> as he has appointed them to be kept. In the primitive times, if a Christian were asked, "Hast thou kept holy the Lord's day?" He would readily answer, "I am a Christian, and dare not do otherwise." (2.) In their whole conversation they <hi type="italic">choose those things that please God.</hi> They do that which is good; they do it with a sincere design to please God in it; they do it of choice, and with delight. If sometimes, through infirmity, they come short in doing that which pleases God, yet they choose it, they endeavour after it, and aim at it. Note, Whatever is God's pleasure should without dispute be our choice. (3.) They <hi type="italic">take hold of his covenant,</hi> and that is a thing that pleases God as much as any thing. The covenant of grace is proposed and proffered to us in the gospel; to take hold of it is to consent to it, to accept the offer and come up to the terms, deliberately and sincerely to take God to be to us a God and to give up ourselves to him to be to him a people. Taking hold of the covenant denotes an entire and resolute consent to it, taking hold as those that are afraid of coming short, catching at it as a good bargain, and as those that are resolved never to let it go, for it is our life: and we take hold of it as a criminal took hold of the horns of the altar to which he fled for refuge. <div eID="gen16831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> 2. What a great deal of comfort they may have if they answer to this character, though they are not built up into families (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Unto them will I give a better place and name.</hi> It is supposed that there is a place and a name, which we have from sons and daughters, that is valuable and desirable. It is a pleasing notion we have that we live in our children when we are dead. But there is a better place, and a better name, which those have that are in covenant with God, and it is sufficient to counterbalance the want of the former. A place and a name denote rest and reputation; a place to live comfortably in themselves, and a name to live creditably with among their neighbours; they shall be happy, and may be easy both at home and abroad. Though they have not children to be the music of their house, or arrows in their quiver, to keep them in countenance when they speak with their enemies in the gate, yet they shall have a place and a name more than equivalent. For, (1.) God will give it to them, will give it to them by promise; he will himself be both their habitation and their glory, their place and their name. (2.) He will give it to them in his house, and within his walls; there they shall have a place, shall be planted so as to take root (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.13">Ps. xcii. 13</reference>), shall <hi type="italic">dwell all the days of their life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Ps. xxvii. 4</reference>. They shall be at home in communion with God, as Anna, that <hi type="italic">departed not from the temple night nor day.</hi> There they shall have a name. A name for the good things with God and good people is a name <hi type="italic">better than that of sons and daughters.</hi> Our relation to God, our interest in Christ, our title to the blessings of the covenant, and our hopes of eternal life, are things that give us in God's house a blessed place and a blessed name. (3.) It shall be <hi type="italic">an everlasting name, that shall never</hi> be extinct, shall never <hi type="italic">be cut off;</hi> like the place and name of angels, who <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> marry not, because they die not. Spiritual blessings are unspeakably better than those of sons and daughters; for children are a certain care and may prove the greatest grief and shame of a man's life, but the blessings we partake of in God's house are a sure and constant joy and honour, comforts which cannot be embittered. <div eID="gen16832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16833" type="x-p"/> II. To those that are themselves the children of strangers. <div eID="gen16833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16834" type="x-p"/> 1. It is here promised that they shall now be welcome to the church, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6-Isa.56.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. When God's Israel come out of Babylon, let them bring as many of their neighbours along with them as they can persuade to come, and God will find room enough for them all in his house. And here, (as before) we may observe, <div eID="gen16834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16835" type="x-p"/> (1.) Upon what terms they shall be welcome. Let them know that God's Israel, when they come out of Babylon, will not be plagued, as they were when they came out of Egypt, with a mixed multitude, that went with them, but were not cordially for them; no, the sons of the strangers shall have a place and a name in God's house provided, [1.] That they forsake other gods, all rivals and pretenders whatsoever, and <hi type="italic">join themselves to the Lord,</hi> so as to become <hi type="italic">one spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.17">1 Cor. vi. 17</reference>. [2.] That they join themselves to him as subjects to their prince and soldiers to their general, by an oath of fidelity and obedience, <hi type="italic">to serve him,</hi> not occasionally, as one would serve a turn, but to be constantly his servants, entirely subject to his command, and devoted to his interest. [3.] That they join themselves to him as friends to his honour and the interests of his kingdom in the world, <hi type="italic">to love the name of the Lord,</hi> to be well pleased with all the discoveries he has made of himself and all the memorials they make of him. Observe, Serving him and loving him go together; for those that love him truly will serve him faithfully, and that obedience is most acceptable to him, as well as most pleasant to us, which flows from a principle of love, for then <hi type="italic">his commandments are not grievous,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.3">1 John v. 3</reference>. [4.] That they keep the sabbath from polluting it; for the stranger that is within thy gates is particularly required to do that. [5.] That they take hold of the covenant, that is, that they come under the bonds of it, and put in for the benefits of it. <div eID="gen16835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16836" type="x-p"/> (2.) To what privileges they shall be welcome, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.7">v. 7</reference>. Three things are here promised them, in their coming to God:—[1.] Assistance: "<hi type="italic">I will bring them to my holy mountain,</hi> not only bid them welcome when they come, but incline them to come, will show them the way, and lead them in it." David himself prays that God by his light and truth would bring them to his <hi type="italic">holy hill,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.43.3">Ps. xliii. 3</reference>. And the sons of the stranger shall be under the same guidance. The church is God's holy hill, on which he hath set his King, and, in bringing them to Zion Hill, he brings them to be subjects to Zion's King, as well as worshippers in Zion's holy temple. [2.] Acceptance: "<hi type="italic">Their burnt-offerings and their sacrifices shall be accepted on my altar,</hi> and be never the less acceptable for being theirs, though they are sons of the stranger." The prayers and praises (those spiritual sacrifices) of devout Gentiles shall be as pleasing to God as those of the pious Jews, and no difference shall be made between them; for, though they are Gentiles by birth, yet through grace they shall be looked upon as the believing seed of faithful Abraham and the praying seed of wrestling Jacob, for in Christ Jesus there is neither Greek nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision. [3.] Comfort. They shall not only be accepted, but they themselves shall have the pleasure of it: <hi type="italic">I will make them joyful in my house of prayer.</hi> They shall have grace, not only to serve God, but to serve him cheerfully and with gladness, and that shall make the service the more acceptable to him; for, when we sing in the ways of the Lord, then great is the glory of our God. They shall go away and <hi type="italic">eat their bread with joy,</hi> because <hi type="italic">God now accepts their works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.7">Eccl. ix. 7</reference>. Nay, though they came mourning to the house of prayer, they shall go away rejoicing, for they shall there find such ease, by casting their cares and burdens upon God, and referring themselves to him, that, like Hannah, they shall go away and their countenance shall be no more sad. Many a sorrowful spirit has been made joyful in the house of prayer. <div eID="gen16836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> 2. It is here promised that multitudes of the Gentiles shall come to the church, not only that the few who come dropping in shall be made welcome, but that great numbers shall come in, and the door be thrown open to them: <hi type="italic">My house shall be called a house of prayer for all people.</hi> The temple was then God's house, and to that Christ applies these words (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">Matt. xxi. 13</reference>), but with an eye to it as a type of the gospel church, <reference osisRef="Heb.9.8-Heb.9.9">Heb. ix. 8, 9</reference>. For Christ calls it <hi type="italic">his house,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.3.6">Heb. iii. 6</reference>. Now concerning this house it is promised, (1.) That it shall not be a house of sacrifice, but a house of prayer. The religious meetings of God's people shall be meetings for prayer, in which they shall join together, as a token of their united faith and mutual love. (2.) That it shall be a house of prayer, not for the people of the Jews only, but for all people. This was fulfilled when Peter was made, not only to perceive it himself, but to tell it to the world, that <hi type="italic">in every nation he that fears God and works righteousness is accepted of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.35">Acts x. 35</reference>. It had been declared again and again that <hi type="italic">the stranger that comes nigh shall be put to death,</hi> but Gentiles shall now be looked upon no longer as strangers and foreigners, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.19">Eph. ii. 19</reference>. And it appears by Solomon's prayer, at the dedication of the temple, both that it was primarily intended for a house of prayer and that strangers should be welcome to it, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.30">1 Kings viii. 30</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.41">41</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.43">43</reference>. And it is intimated here (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">v. 8</reference>) that when the Gentiles are called in they shall be incorporated into one body with the Jews, that (as Christ says, <reference osisRef="John.10.16">John x. 16</reference>) there may be <hi type="italic">one fold and one Shepherd;</hi> for, [1.] God will <hi type="italic">gather the outcasts of Israel.</hi> Many of the Jews that had by their unbelief cast themselves out shall by faith be brought in again, <hi type="italic">a remnant according to the election of grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">Rom. xi. 5</reference>. Christ came to the <hi type="italic">lost sheep of the house of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.24">Matt. xv. 24</reference>), to <hi type="italic">gather their outcasts</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">Ps. cxlvii. 2</reference>), to <hi type="italic">restore their preserved</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.6">ch. xlix. 6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">to be their glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.2.32">Luke ii. 32</reference>. [2.] He will gather others also to him, besides his own outcasts that are gathered to him. Or, though some of the Gentiles have come over now and then into the church, that shall not serve (as some may think) to answer the extent of these promises; no, there are still more and more to be brought in: "<hi type="italic">I will gather others to him besides these;</hi> these are but the first-fruits in comparison with the harvest that shall be gathered for Christ in the nations of the earth, when the fulness of the Gentiles shall come in." Note, The church is a growing body: when some are gathered to it we may still hope there shall be more, till the mystical body be completed. <hi type="italic">Other sheep I have.</hi>
entries.d095ca375ec2858fce4c9ee99bb8402da392cebf: <div eID="gen16837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Charge against the Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> All ye beasts of the field, come to devour, <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> all ye beasts in the forest. <hi type="super">10</hi> His watchmen <hi type="italic">are</hi> blind: they are all ignorant, they <hi type="italic">are</hi> all dumb dogs, they cannot bark; sleeping, lying down, loving to slumber. <hi type="super">11</hi> Yea, <hi type="italic">they are</hi> greedy dogs <hi type="italic">which</hi> can never have enough, and they <hi type="italic">are</hi> shepherds <hi type="italic">that</hi> cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter. <hi type="super">12</hi> Come ye, <hi type="italic">say they,</hi> I will fetch wine, and we will fill ourselves with strong drink; and to morrow shall be as this day, <hi type="italic">and</hi> much more abundant. <div eID="gen16838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16839" type="x-p"/> From words of comfort the prophet here, by a very sudden change of his style, passes to words of reproof and conviction, and goes on in that strain, for the most part, in the three following chapters; and therefore some here begin a new sermon. He had assured the people that in due time God would deliver them out of captivity, which was designed for the comfort of those that should live when God would do this. Now here he shows what their sins and provocations were, for which God would send them into captivity, and this was designed for the conviction of those that lived in his own time, nearly a hundred years before the captivity, who were now filling up the measure of the nation's sin, and to justify God in what he brought upon them. God will lay them waste by the fierceness of their enemies, for the falseness of their friends. <div eID="gen16839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16840" type="x-p"/> I. Desolating judgments are here summoned, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">v. 9</reference>. The sheep of God's pasture are now to be made the sheep of his slaughter, to fall as victims to his justice, and therefore <hi type="italic">the beasts of the field and the forest</hi> are called to come and devour. They are beasts of prey, and do it from their own ravenous disposition; but God permits them to do it, nay, he employs them as his servants in doing it, the ministers of his justice, though they mean not so, neither does their heart think so. If this refers primarily to the descent made upon them by the Babylonians, and their devouring them, yet it may look further, to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish nation by the Romans, after these outcasts of them (mentioned <reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">v. 8</reference>) were gathered in to the Christian church. The Roman armies came upon them as beasts of the forest to devour them, and they quite <hi type="italic">took away their place and nation.</hi> Note, When God has bloody work to do he has beasts of prey within call, to be employed in doing it. <div eID="gen16840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16841" type="x-p"/> II. The reason of these judgments is here given. The shepherds, who should have been the watchmen of the flock, to discover the approaches of the beasts of prey, to keep them off, and protect the sheep, were treacherous and careless, minded not their business, nor made any conscience of the trust reposed in them, and so the sheep became an easy prey to the wild beasts. Now this may refer to the false prophets that lived in Isaiah's, Jeremiah's, and Ezekiel's time (who flattered the people in their wicked ways, and told them they should have peace though they went on) and to the priests that bore rule by their means. Or it may refer to the wicked princes, the sons of Josiah, that <hi type="italic">did evil in the sight of the Lord,</hi> and other wicked magistrates under them, who betrayed their trust, were vicious and profane, and, instead of making up the breach at which the judgments of God were breaking in upon them, made it wider, and augmented the fierce anger of the Lord instead of doing any thing to turn it away. They should have kept judgment and justice (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.1">v. 1</reference>), but they abandoned both, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.1">Jer. v. 1</reference>. Or it may refer to those who were the nation's watchmen in our Saviour's time, the chief priests and the scribes, who should have discerned the signs of the times and have given notice to the people of the approach of the Messiah, but who, instead of that, opposed him, and did all they could to keep people from coming to the knowledge of him and to prejudice them against him. It is a very sad character that is here given of these watchmen. <hi type="italic">Woe unto thee, O land!</hi> when thy guides are such. 1. They had no sense or knowledge of their business. They were wretchedly ignorant of their work, and very unfit to teach, being so ill-taught themselves: <hi type="italic">His watchmen are blind,</hi> and therefore utterly unfit to be watchmen. If the seers see not, who shall see for us? <hi type="italic">If the light that is in us be darkness, how great is that darkness!</hi> Christ describes the Pharisees to be <hi type="italic">blind leaders of the blind,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.15.14">Matt. xv. 14</reference>. The beasts of the field come to devour, and the watchmen are blind, and are not aware of them. <hi type="italic">They are all ignorant</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">v. 10</reference>), <hi type="italic">shepherds that cannot understand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">v. 11</reference>), that know not what is to be done about the sheep, nor can <hi type="italic">feed them with understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.15">Jer. iii. 15</reference>. 2. What little knowledge they had they made no use of it; no one was the better for it. As they were blind watchmen, that could not discern the danger, so they were <hi type="italic">dumb dogs,</hi> that would not give warning of it. And why are the dogs set to guard the sheep if they cannot bark to waken the shepherd and frighten the wolf? Such were these; those that had the charge of souls never reproved men for their faults, nor told them what would be in the end thereof, never gave them notice of the judgments of God that were breaking in upon them. They barked at God's prophets, and bit them too, and worried the sheep, but made no opposition to the wolf or thief. 3. They were very lazy, and would take no pains. They loved their ease, and hated business, were always <hi type="italic">sleeping, lying down</hi> and <hi type="italic">loving to slumber.</hi> They were not overcome and overpowered by sleep, as the disciples, through grief and fatigue, but they lay down on purpose to invite sleep, and said, <hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease. Yet a little sleep.</hi> It is bad with a people when their shepherds slumber (<reference osisRef="Nah.3.18">Nah. iii. 18</reference>), and it is well for God's people that their shepherd, the keeper of Israel, neither slumbers nor sleeps. 4. They were very covetous and eager after the world—<hi type="italic">greedy dogs that can never have enough.</hi> If they had ever so much, they would think it too little. They so love silver as never to be satisfied with silver, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.10">Eccl. v. 10</reference>. All their enquiry is what they shall get, not what they shall do. Let them have the wages, and they care not whether the work be done or no; they feed not the flock, but fleece it. They are every one looking to his <hi type="italic">own way,</hi> minding his own private interests, and have no regard at all to the public welfare. It was St. Paul's complaint of the watchmen in his time (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.21">Phil. ii. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">All seek their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ's.</hi> Every one is for propagating his own opinion, advancing his own party, raising his own family, and having every thing to his own mind, while the common concerns of the public are wretchedly neglected and postponed. They look <hi type="italic">every one to his gain from his quarter,</hi> from his end or part of the work. They are for fain from every quarter (<hi type="italic">Rem rem quocunque modo rem—Money, money, by fair means or by foul we must have money</hi>), but especially from their own quarter, where they will be sure to take care that they lose nothing, nor miss any thing that is to be got. If any one put not into their mouths they not only will do him no service, but they <hi type="italic">prepare war against him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.5">Mic. iii. 5</reference>. 5. They were perfect epicures, given to their pleasures, never so much in their element as in their drunken revels (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">Come</hi> (say they), <hi type="italic">I will fetch wine</hi> (they have that at command; their cellars are better furnished than their closets) <hi type="italic">and we will fill ourselves,</hi> or be drunk, <hi type="italic">with strong drink.</hi> They were often drunk, not overseen (as we say) or overtaken in drink, but designedly. The watchmen did thus invite and encourage one another to drink to excess, or they courted the people to sit and drink with them, and so confirmed those in their wicked ways, and hardened their hearts, whom they should have reproved. How could they think it any harm to be drunk when the watchmen themselves joined with them and led them to it! 6. They were very secure and confident of the continuance of their prosperity and ease; they said, "<hi type="italic">To-morrow shall be as this day and much more abundant;</hi> we shall have as much to spend upon our lusts to-morrow as we have to-day." They had no thought at all of their own frailty and mortality, though they were shortening their days and hastening their deaths by their excesses. They had no dread of the judgments of God, though they were daily provoking him and making themselves liable to his wrath and curse. They never considered the uncertainty of all the delights and enjoyments of sense, how they perish in the using and pass away with the lusts of them. They resolved to continue in this wicked course, whatever their consciences said to the contrary, to be as merry to-morrow as they are to-day. <hi type="italic">But boast not thyself of to-morrow</hi> when perhaps <hi type="italic">this night thy soul shall be required of thee.</hi>  <chapter eID="Isa.56"/> <div eID="gen16841" type="x-p"/>

entries.52794e7c6e1c5d0e63fd1b45fabca5c6dcf69fa8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9380"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 56</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.12">Is 56:1-12</reference>. The Preparation Needed on the Part of Those Who Wish to Be Admitted to the Kingdom of God.</title> <div sID="gen16210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9380"/><hi type="bold">1. judgment--</hi>equity. John the Baptist preached similarly a return to righteousness, as needed to prepare men for Messiah's first coming (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.3">Lu 3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.3.8-Luke.3.14">8-14</reference>). So it shall be before the second coming (Mal 4:4-6).<div eID="gen16210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">near to come--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.3.2">Mt 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.4.17">4:17</reference>), also as to the second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.10">Is 62:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.62.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Lu 21:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.13.11">Ro 13:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.25">He 10:25</reference>).<div eID="gen16211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">righteousness--</hi>answering to "salvation" in the parallel clause; therefore it means righteousness which bringeth salvation (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">Is 46:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.25">Ro 3:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.26">26</reference>). <div eID="gen16212" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a7877b44c55157f92be8d140f357ef3d2641ae9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9381"/><div sID="gen16213" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9381"/>2. (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.43">Lu 12:43</reference>).<div eID="gen16213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the man--</hi>Hebrew, enosh, "a man in humble life," in contradistinction to Hebrew, ish, "one of high rank." Even the humblest, as "the stranger" and "the eunuch" (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.4">Is 56:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">6</reference>), are admissible to these privileges.<div eID="gen16214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">this ... it--</hi>what follows: "keeping the Sabbath," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Is 58:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.58.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.12">Eze 20:12</reference>). A proof that the Sabbath, in the spirit of its obligation, was to be binding under the Gospel (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.23">Is 66:23</reference>). That gospel times are referred to is plain, from the blessing not being pronounced on the man who observed the sacrificial ritual of the Jewish law.<div eID="gen16215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16216" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">layeth hold--</hi>image from one grasping firmly some precious object which he is afraid of having forcibly snatched from him. The "Sabbath" here includes all the ordinances of divine worship under the new gospel law.<div eID="gen16216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">keepeth ... hand ... from ... evil--</hi>The observance of the second table of the law; as the "Sabbath" referred to the first table. Together, they form the whole duty of man, the worship of God and a holy life. <div eID="gen16217" type="x-p"/>
entries.5c1082b5cf2b2d94e97f8fcef233b138f8d94bd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9382"/><div sID="gen16218" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9382"/>3. God welcomes all believers, without distinction of persons, under the new economy (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.34">Ac 10:34</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.35">35</reference>).<div eID="gen16218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16219" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joined ... to ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Num.18.4">Nu 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.18.7">7</reference>). "Proselytes."<div eID="gen16219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16220" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">separated--</hi>Proselytes from the Gentiles were not admitted to the same privileges as native Israelites. This barrier between Jews and Gentiles was to be broken down (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14-Eph.2.16">Ep 2:14-16</reference>).<div eID="gen16220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eunuch--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Acts.8.27">Ac 8:27</reference>, &c.). Eunuchs were chamberlains over harems, or court ministers in general.<div eID="gen16221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dry tree--</hi>barren (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.23.31">Lu 23:31</reference>); not admissible into the congregation of Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.1-Deut.23.3">De 23:1-3</reference>). Under the Gospel the eunuch and stranger should be released from religious and civil disabilities. <div eID="gen16222" type="x-p"/>
entries.162af7b3bef9cd8ea82670843451415989f2baff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9383"/><div sID="gen16223" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9383"/><hi type="bold">4. please me--</hi>sacrifice their own pleasure to mine.<div eID="gen16223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">take hold--</hi>so "layeth hold" (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.56.2">Is 56:2</reference>). <div eID="gen16224" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1077d5c1cf35c5de9e69f0a7975cf587ec4b2d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9384"/><div sID="gen16225" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9384"/><hi type="bold">5. in mine house--</hi>the temple, the emblem of the Church (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>). They shall no longer be confined as proselytes were, to the outer court, but shall be admitted "into the holiest" (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.19">He 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.20">20</reference>).<div eID="gen16225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a place--</hi>literally, "a hand."<div eID="gen16226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16227" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">than of sons--</hi>Though the eunuch is barren of children (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Is 56:3</reference>), I will give him a more lasting name than that of being father of sons and daughters (regarded as a high honor among the Hebrews) (<reference osisRef="John.1.12">Joh 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.3">10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.1">1Jo 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.17">Re 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen16227" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d675f972a96932449418107b7539011bc9ec65c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9385"/><div sID="gen16228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9385"/><hi type="bold">6. join ... Lord--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jr 50:6</reference>). Conditions of admission to the privileges of adoption. <div eID="gen16228" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a29f84e2fb6d58e03eddc7507ada3c23a219acb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9386"/><div sID="gen16229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9386"/><hi type="bold">7. Even them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.2.11-Eph.2.13">Ep 2:11-13</reference>).<div eID="gen16229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16230" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to my holy mountain--</hi>Jerusalem, the seat of the Lord's throne in His coming kingdom (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2">Is 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.17">Jr 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">joyful--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.5.11">Ro 5:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burnt offerings ... sacrifices--</hi>spiritual, of which the literal were types (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>).<div eID="gen16232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accepted--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.6">Ep 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen16233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">altar--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">He 13:10</reference>), spiritually, the Cross of Christ, which sanctifies our sacrifices of prayer and praise.<div eID="gen16234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">house ... for all people--</hi>or rather, "peoples." No longer restricted to one favored people (Mal 1:11; <reference osisRef="John.4.21">Joh 4:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.8">1Ti 2:8</reference>). To be fully realized at the second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.2-Isa.2.4">Is 2:2-4</reference>). No longer literal, but spiritual sacrifice, namely, "prayer" shall be offered (<reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">Psa 141:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">51:17</reference>; Mal 1:11; <reference osisRef="Matt.21.13">Mt 21:13</reference>). <div eID="gen16235" type="x-p"/>
entries.70cd8acf8d7a9fe019fd2be74c11db2c844a3685: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9387"/><div sID="gen16236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9387"/>8. Jehovah will not only restore the scattered outcasts of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Is 11:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">Psa 147:2</reference>) to their own land, but "will gather others ('strangers') to him (Israel), besides those gathered" (Margin, "to his gathered"; that is, in addition to the Israelites collected from their dispersion), (<reference osisRef="John.10.16">Joh 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Ep 1:10</reference>; 2:19). <div eID="gen16236" type="x-p"/>
entries.681c97cf4cd65bdc7c73e846f21c4b6877064a1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9388"/><div sID="gen16237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9388"/><hi type="bold">9. beasts--</hi>Gentile idolatrous nations hostile to the Jews, summoned by God to chastise them (Jr 12:7-9; 50:<reference osisRef="Jer.9.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>): the Chaldeans and subsequently the Romans. The mention of the "outcasts of Israel" (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">Is 56:8</reference>) brings in view the outcasting, caused by the sins of their rulers (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.10-Isa.56.12">Is 56:10-12</reference>).<div eID="gen16237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to devour--</hi>namely, Israel. <div eID="gen16238" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c278de560580526058082070cdb5019182e0d62: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9389"/><div sID="gen16239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9389"/><hi type="bold">10. His watchmen--</hi>Israel's spiritual leaders (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Is 62:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>).<div eID="gen16239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dumb dogs--</hi>image from bad shepherds' watchdogs, which fail to give notice, by barking, of the approach of wild beasts.<div eID="gen16240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16241" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blind--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Matt.23.16">Mt 23:16</reference>).<div eID="gen16241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sleeping, lying down--</hi>rather, "dreamers, sluggards" [Lowth]. Not merely sleeping inactive, but under visionary delusions.<div eID="gen16242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loving to slumber--</hi>not merely slumbering involuntarily, but loving it. <div eID="gen16243" type="x-p"/>
entries.604a00a7ec0760a6255c5ecb9ea27d2396dd03d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9390"/><div sID="gen16244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9390"/><hi type="bold">11. greedy--</hi>literally, "strong" (that is, insatiable) in appetite (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Eze 34:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cannot understand--</hi>unable to comprehend the wants of the people, spiritually: so <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10">Is 56:10</reference>, "cannot bark."<div eID="gen16245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">look to ... own way--</hi>that is, their own selfish interests; not to the spiritual welfare of the people (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.13">Jr 6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.22.27">Eze 22:27</reference>).<div eID="gen16246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from his quarter--</hi>rather, "from the highest to the lowest" [Lowth]. "From his quarter"; that is, from one end to the other of them, one and all (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.4">Ge 19:4</reference>). <div eID="gen16247" type="x-p"/>
entries.e12d35d3316cd880ea5b397f11e6c2c29fce8987: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9391"/><div sID="gen16248" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9391"/><hi type="bold">12. fetch wine--</hi>language of the national teachers challenging one another to drink. Barnes translates, "I will take another cup" (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Is 5:11</reference>).<div eID="gen16248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to-morrow, &c.--</hi>Their self-indulgence was habitual and intentional: not merely they drink, but they mean to continue so. <chapter eID="Isa.56"/>

entries.36a6d72d0ab1d90a9d71e23f780a7e8838066ed4: <div eID="gen28720" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen28721" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28722" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28722" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen28721" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen28723" type="x-p"/> Whoever would partake of the blessings of the Gospel is required to be holy in all manner of life and conversation. And he that will be so is declared to be accepted according to this gracious dispensation, the blessings of which are large as the human race, without any respect to persons or to nations, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.8">Isa 56:1-8</reference>. At the ninth verse begins a different subject, or new section of prophecy. It opens with calling on the enemies of the Jews, (the Chaldeans, or perhaps the Romans), as beasts of prey against them, for the sins of their rulers, teachers, and other profane people among them, whose guilt drew down judgments on the nation, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9-Isa.56.12">Isa 56:9-12</reference>.
entries.9122c739ab359bef9f930be05a5cccfd92d38e29: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen28723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28724" type="x-p"/> That keepeth the Sabbath from polluting it - Kimchi has an excellent note here. "The Sabbath is sanctified when it is distinguished in dignity; and separated from other days. <div eID="gen28724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28725" type="x-p"/> 1. As to the body, in meat, drink, and clean clothing. <div eID="gen28725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28726" type="x-p"/> 2. As to the soul, that it be empty of worldly occupations, and be busily employed in the words of the law and wisdom, and in meditation on the works of the Lord." <div eID="gen28726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28727" type="x-p"/> The rabbins say, "Jerusalem had never been destroyed, had not the Sabbaths been profaned in it."
entries.e87ea06c09df8f3ba2f8c02ad4df3b15de45f44a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen28727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28728" type="x-p"/> I will give them an everlasting name - For לו lo, him, in the singular, it is evident that we ought to read למו lamo, them, in the plural: so read the Septuagint, Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate.
entries.68cdae351022c1bb771beb29b33dfd31aefe0c34: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen28728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28729" type="x-p"/> The sons of the stranger - The Gentiles. <div eID="gen28729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28730" type="x-p"/> That join themselves to the Lord - Who shall enter into the Christian covenant by baptism and faith in Christ, as the Jews and proselytes did by circumcision. <div eID="gen28730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28731" type="x-p"/> To serve him - To live according to the Gospel, and ever do that which is right in the sight of the Lord. <div eID="gen28731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28732" type="x-p"/> To love the name of the Lord - The name of Jesus, the Christ, the Savior of sinners, the Anointed of God, and the Giver of the Holy Spirit to his followers. <div eID="gen28732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28733" type="x-p"/> To be his servants - To worship no other God but Jehovah, and to trust in none for salvation but his Christ. <div eID="gen28733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28734" type="x-p"/> That keepeth the Sabbath - That observes it as a type of the rest that remains for the people of God. <div eID="gen28734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28735" type="x-p"/> And taketh hold of my covenant - בבריתי biberithi, "of my covenant sacrifice;" as without this he can do nothing good; and without it nothing can be acceptable to the infinite majesty of the Most High.
entries.bf2c78802dee1a8961ff2d23979abefcdb64d0a9: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen28735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28736" type="x-p"/> Shall be accepted - A word is here lost out of the text: it is supplied from the Septuagint, יהיו yihyu, εσονται, "they shall be." - Houbigant.
entries.d29c30dc750658b41570ec7abf705b17d6784405: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen28736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28737" type="x-p"/> All ye beasts of the field - Here manifestly begins a new section. The prophet in the foregoing chapters, having comforted the faithful Jews with many great promises of God's favor to be extended to them, in the restoration of their ruined state, and in the enlargement of his Church by the admission of the Gentiles; here on a sudden makes a transition to the more disagreeable part of the prospect, and to a sharp reproof of the wicked and unbelievers; and especially of the negligent and faithless governors and teachers, of the idolaters and hypocrites, who would still draw down his judgments upon the nation. Probably having in view the destruction of their city and polity by the Chaldeans, and perhaps by the Romans. The same subject is continued in the next chapter; in which the charge of corruption and apostasy becomes more general against the whole Jewish Church. Some expositors have made great difficulties in the 9th verse of this chapter, where there seems to be none. It is perfectly well explained by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.7">Jer 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.9">Jer 12:9</reference>, where, having introduced God declaring his purpose of punishing his people, by giving them up as a prey to their enemies the Chaldeans, a charge to these his agents is given in words very nearly the same with those of Isaiah in this place: - "I have forsaken my house; I have deserted my heritage; <div eID="gen28737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28738" type="x-p"/> I have given up the beloved of my soul into the hands of her enemies. - <div eID="gen28738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28739" type="x-p"/> Come away, be gathered together, all ye beasts of the field; <div eID="gen28739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28740" type="x-p"/> Come away to devour." <div eID="gen28740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28741" type="x-p"/> All ye beasts in the forest "All ye beasts of the forest" - Instead of ביער baiyaar, three MSS. have יער yaar, without the preposition; which seems to be right, and is confirmed by all the ancient Versions.
entries.3f41cbf1b42e03a50b0e121e532b9e39b4a11d17: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen28741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28742" type="x-p"/> His watchmen are blind - Kimchi observes, "The flock is intrusted to the care of these watchmen. The wild beasts come; these dogs bark not; and the wild beasts devour the flock. Thus they do not profit the flock. Yea, they injure it; for the owner trusts in them, that they will watch and be faithful; but they are not. These are the false teachers and careless shepherds." <div eID="gen28742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28743" type="x-p"/> Dumb dogs, they cannot bark - See note on <reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Isa 62:6</reference>. <div eID="gen28743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28744" type="x-p"/> Sleeping "Dreamers" - הזים hozim, ενυπνιαζομενοι, Septuagint. This seems to be the best authority for the meaning of this word, which occurs only in this place: but it is to be observed, that eleven MSS. of Kennicott's and De Rossi's, and four editions, have חזים chazim, seers, or those who see; and so the Vulgate seems to have read, videntes vana, "seeing vain things." <div eID="gen28744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28745" type="x-p"/> Loving to slumber - לנום lanum: but six of Kennicott's and seven of De Rossi's MSS. read לנוס lanus, to fly, "to change their residence:" but what connection such reading can have with the sense of the passage, I cannot discern. What is taken for ס samech here is, I have no doubt, a narrow formed final ם mem, which has been mistaken for the above. Many instances occur in my own MSS., where the final ם mem is similar to the samech; and yet no such change was intended by the scribe.
entries.673d6055e2063df601c580bd3a7d98a319f709c5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen28745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28746" type="x-p"/> Greedy dogs - Insatiably feeding themselves with the fat, and clothing themselves with the wool, while the flock is scattered, ravaged, and starved! O what an abundance of these dumb and greedy dogs are there found hanging on and prowling about the flock of Christ! How can any careless, avaricious, hireling minister read this without agitation and dismay?
entries.2b9ab2b47efd45bdef0c750360256947fbc6dba0: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen28746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28747" type="x-p"/> I will fetch wine "Let us provide wine" - For אקחה ekchah, first person singular, an ancient MS. has נקחה nikchah, first person plural; and another ancient MS. has אק ak upon a rasure. So the Syriac, Chaldee, and Vulgate render it. The spirit of this Epicurean sentiment is this: Let us indulge ourselves in the present time to the utmost, and instead of any gloomy forebodings of the future, let us expect nothing but increasing hilarity for every day we shall live. Thus they, "Counting on long years of pleasure here, <div eID="gen28747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28748" type="x-p"/> Are quite unfurnished for the world to come."  <chapter eID="Isa.56"/> <div eID="gen28748" type="x-p"/>

entries.e7ae87b46e1085731d3f41e7ba2b44f07033bb49: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.2">Isa 56:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen13552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> The note of admonition struck in the foregoing prophecy is continued here, the sabbatical duties being enforced with especial emphasis as part of the general righteousness of life. <hi type="italic">“Thus saith Jehovah, Keep ye right, and do righteousness: for my salvation is near to come, and my righteousness to reveal itself. Blessed is the mortal that doeth this, and the son of man that layeth fast hold thereon; who keepeth the Sabbath, that he doth not desecrate it, and keepeth his hand from doing any kind of evil.”</hi> Jehovah and Israel have both an objective standard in the covenant relation into which they have entered: משׁפּט (right) is practice answering to this; ישׁוּעה (salvation) the performance promised by God; צדקה (righteousness) on both sides such personal activity as is in accordance with the covenant relation, or what is the same thing, with the purpose and plan of salvation. The nearer the full realization on the part of Jehovah of what He has promised, the more faithful ought Israel to be in everything to which it is bound by its relation to Jehovah. זאת (this) points, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.7.4">Psa 7:4</reference>, to what follows; and so also does בּהּ, which points back to זאת. Instead of שׁמור or לשׁמר we have here שׁמר, the זאת being described personally instead of objectively. שּׁבּת is used as a masculine in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.2">Isa 56:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">Isa 56:6</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.58.13">Isa 58:13</reference>), although the word is not formed after the same manner as קטּל, but is rather contracted from שׁבּתת (a festive time, possibly with עת = עדת understood), and therefore was originally a feminine; and it is so personified in the language employed in the worship of the synagogue.<note placement="foot">According to <hi type="italic">b. Sabbath</hi> 119 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, R. Chanina dressed himself on Friday evening in his sabbath-clothes, and said, “Come, and let us go to meet Queen Sabbath.” And so did also Jannai, saying, “Come, O bride; come, O bride.” Hence the customary song with which the Sabbath was greeted had נקבּלה שׁבּת פּני כּלּה לקראת דודי לכה as it commencement and refrain.</note>
entries.2a7953c95c0fa7b93ac8d4dfaeeaf141fdb9b6b4: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa 56:3</reference> <div eID="gen13553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> The אשרי (blessed) of <reference osisRef="Isa.56.2">Isa 56:2</reference> is now extended to those who might imagine that they had no right to console themselves with the promises which it contained. <hi type="italic">“And let not the foreigner, who hath not joined himself to Jehovah, speak thus: Assuredly Jehovah will cut me off from His people; and let not the eunuch say, I am only a dry tree.”</hi> As נלוה is not pointed as a participle (נלוה), but as a 3rd pers. pres., the ה of הנּלוה is equivalent to אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Josh.10.24">Jos 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.18.21">Gen 18:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.21.3">Gen 21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.27">Gen 46:27</reference>; 1Ki 11:9 (Ges. §109). By the eunuchs we are to understand those of Israelitish descent, as the attributive clause is not repeated in their case. Heathen, who professed the religion of Jehovah, and had attached themselves to Israel, might be afraid lest, when Israel should be restored to its native land, according to the promise, as a holy and glorious community with a thoroughly priestly character, Jehovah would no longer tolerate them, i.e., would forbid their receiving full citizenship. יבדּילני has the connecting vowel <hi type="italic">á</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.19">Gen 19:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32">Gen 29:32</reference>, instead of the usual <hi type="italic">ē</hi>. And the Israelitish eunuchs, who had been mutilated against their will, that they might serve at heathen courts or in the houses of foreign lords, and therefore had not been unfaithful to Jehovah, might be afraid lest, as unfruitful trees, they should be pronounced unworthy of standing in the congregation of Jehovah. There was more ground for the anxiety of the latter than for that of the former. For the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.4-Deut.23.7">Deu 23:4-7</reference> merely prohibits Ammonites and Moabites for all time to come from reception into the congregation, on account of their unbrotherly conduct towards the Israelites as they came out of Egypt, whilst that in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.8-Deut.23.9">Deu 23:8-9</reference> prohibits the reception of Edomites and Egyptians to the third generation; so that there was no prohibition as to other allies - such, for example, as the Babylonians. On the other hand, the law in <reference osisRef="Deut.23.2">Deu 23:2</reference> expressly declares, as an expression of the horror of God at any such mutilation of nature, and for the purpose of precluding it, that no kind of emasculated person is to enter the congregation of Jehovah. But prophecy breaks through these limits of the law.
entries.36ba2c165e46a8e370ef83153516a9685e06565d: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.4-Isa.56.5">Isa 56:4-5</reference> <hi type="italic">“For thus saith Jehovah to the circumcised, Those who keep my Sabbaths, and decide for that in which I take pleasure, and take fast hold of my covenant; I give to them in my house and within my walls a memorial and a name better than sons and daughters: I give such a man an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off.”</hi> The second condition after the sanctification of the Sabbath has reference to the regulation of life according to the revealed will of God; the third to fidelity with regard to the covenant of circumcision. יד also means a side, and hence a place (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.13">Deu 23:13</reference>); but in the passage before us, where ושׁם יד form a closely connected pair of words, to which וּמבּנות מבּנים is appended, it signifies the memorial, equivalent to מצּבת   (2 Sam 18; 1:1-24:25; <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.12">1Sa 15:12</reference>), as an index lifted up on high (<reference osisRef="Ezek.21.24">Eze 21:24</reference>), which strikes the eye and arrests attention, pointing like a signpost to the person upon whom it is placed, like <hi type="italic">monumentum a monendo</hi>. They are assured that they will not be excluded from close fellowship with the church (“in my house and within my walls”), and also promised, as a superabundant compensation for the want of posterity, long life in the memory of future ages, by whom their long tried attachment to Jehovah and His people in circumstances of great temptation will not be forgotten.
entries.957823776658a56c1210652dd09e9155808c24fa: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6-Isa.56.7">Isa 56:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen13554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> The fears of proselytes from among the heathen are also removed. <hi type="italic">“And the foreigners, who have joined themselves to Jehovah, to serve Him, and to love the name of Jehovah, to be His servants, whoever keepeth the Sabbath from desecrating it, and those who hold fast to my covenant, I bring them to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer; their whole-offerings and their slain-offerings are well-pleasing upon mine altar: for my house, a house of prayer shall it be called for all nations.”</hi> The proselytes, who have attached themselves to Jehovah (על־הא),<note placement="foot">The oriental reading, not in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.3">Isa 56:3</reference>, but here in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.6">Isa 56:6</reference>, is על־ה; the western, אל־ה. The Masora follows the western (מערבאי( nre), i.e., the Palestinian, and reckons this passage as one of the 31 על־ה in the Old Testament Scriptures.</note> the God of Israel, with the pure intention of serving Him with love, are not to be left behind in the strange land. Jehovah will bring them along with His people to the holy mountain, upon which His temple rises once more; there will He cause them to rejoice, and all that they place upon His altar will find a most gracious acceptance. It is impossible that the prophet should be thinking here of the worship of the future without sacrifice, although in <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">Isa 53:1-12</reference> he predicts the self-sacrifice of the “Servant of Jehovah,” which puts an end to all animals sacrifices. But here the temple is called “the house of prayer,” from the prayer which is the soul of all worship. It will be called a house of prayer for all nations; and therefore its nature will correspond to its name. This ultimate intention is already indicated in Solomon’s dedicatory prayer (1Ki 8:41-43); but our prophet was the first to give it this definite universal expression. Throughout this passage the spirit of the law is striving to liberate itself from its bondage. Nor is there anything to surprise us in the breaking down of the party wall, built up so absolutely between the eunuchs on the one hand and the congregation on the other, or the one partially erected between the heathen and the congregation of Israel; as we may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.66.21">Isa 66:21</reference>, where it is affirmed that Jehovah will even take priests and Levites out of the midst of the heathen whom Israel will bring back with it into its own land.
entries.1f8f8e93413c5462c9404084b6394395d4707669: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.8">Isa 56:8</reference> <div eID="gen13555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> The expression “<hi type="italic">saying of the Lord</hi>” (<hi type="italic">Ne'um Jehovah</hi>), which is so solemn an expression in itself, and which stands here at the head of the following declaration, is a proof that it contains not only something great, but something which needs a solemn confirmation because of its strangeness. Not only is there no ground for supposing that Gentiles who love Jehovah will be excluded from the congregation; but it is really Jehovah’s intention to gather some out of the heathen, and add them to the assembled diaspora of Israel. <hi type="italic">“Word of the Lord, Jehovah: gathering the outcasts of Israel, I will also gather beyond itself to its gathered ones.”</hi> We only find ה נאם at the commencement of the sentence, in this passage and Zec 12:1. The double name of God, <hi type="italic">Adonai Jehovah</hi>, also indicates something great. עליו (to it) refers to Israel, and לנקבּציו is an explanatory permutative, equivalent to על־נקבציו; or else על denotes the fact that the gathering will exceed the limits of Israel (cf., <reference osisRef="Gen.48.22">Gen 48:22</reference>), and ל the addition that will be made to the gathered ones of Israel. The meaning in either case remains the same. Jehovah here declares what Jesus says in Joh 10:16 : “Other sheep I have which are not of this fold: them also I must bring, and they shall hear my voice; and there shall be one fold and one Shepherd:” “Jehovah one, and His name one,” as it is expressed in Zec 14:9. Such as the views and hopes that have grown up out of the chastisement inflicted by their captivity. God has made it a preparatory school for New Testament times. It has been made subservient to the bursting of the fetters of the law, the liberation of the spirit of the law, and the establishment of friendship between Israel and the Gentile world as called to one common salvation.
entries.2d585c6605a66e263054ffd7a9f19e6486ae0907: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">Isa 56:9</reference> <div eID="gen13556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> It is a question whether <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">Isa 56:9</reference> forms the commencement of a fresh prophecy, or merely the second half of the prophecy contained in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1">Isa 56:1</reference>-8. We decide, for our part, in favour of the former. If Isa 56:9. formed an antithetical second half to the promising first half in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.1-Isa.56.8">Isa 56:1-8</reference>, we should expect to find the prophets and leaders of Israel, whose licentiousness and want of principle are here so severely condemned, threatened with destruction in the heathen land, whilst true proselytes and even eunuchs were brought to the holy mountain. But we meet with this antithesis for the first time in <reference osisRef="Isa.57.13">Isa 57:13</reference>, where we evidently find ourselves in the midst of another prophetic address. And where can that address commence, if not at <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">Isa 56:9</reference>, from which point onwards we have that hard, dull, sharp, and concise language of strong indignation, which recals to mind psalms written “in a thundering style” (<hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, i. 80) and the reproachful addresses of Jeremiah, and which passes again in Isa 57:11. into the lofty crystalline language peculiar to our prophet’s “book of consolation?” The new prophetic address commences, like <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa 55:1</reference>, with a summons. <hi type="italic">“All ye beasts of the field, come near! To devour, all ye beasts in the forest!”</hi> According to the accentuation before us (לכל <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>, כלח־יתו <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>), the beasts of the field are summoned to devour the beasts in the forest. This accentuation, however, is false, and must be exchanged for another which is supported by some MSS, viz., לכל <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, כלח־יתו <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>, and ביער <hi type="italic">Beth raphatum</hi>. It is true that even with these accents we might still adhere to the view favoured by Jewish commentators, viz., that the beasts of the field are to be devoured by the beasts of the forest, if this view yielded any admissible sense (compare, for example, that supported by Meyer, “Ye enemies, devour the scattered ones of my congregation”), and had not against it the synonymous parallelism of שדי חיתו and ביער חיתו (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.20">Isa 43:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.11">Psa 104:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.20">Psa 104:20</reference>; cf., <reference osisRef="Gen.3.14">Gen 3:14</reference>). But there remains another view, according to which ביער כל־חיתו is a second vocative answering to שׂדי כל־חיתו. According to the Targum, what is to be devoured is the great body of heathen kings attacking Jerusalem; according to Jerome, Cyril, Stier, etc., the pasture and food provided by the grace of God. But what follows teaches us something different from this. Israel has prophets and shepherds, who are blind to every coming danger, and therefore fail to give warning of its approach, because they are sunken in selfishness and debauchery. It resembles a flock with a keeper, and therefore an easy prey (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>); and the meaning of the appeal, which is certainly addressed to the nations of the world, the enemies of the people of God, is this: “Ye have only to draw near; ye can feed undisturbed, and devour as much as ye please.” This is the explanation adopted by most of the more modern commentators. In <reference osisRef="Jer.12.9">Jer 12:9</reference>, which is founded upon this (“Assemble all ye beasts of the field, bring them hither to devour”), it is also Jerusalem which is assigned as food to the heathen. The parallel in <reference osisRef="Isa.56.9">Isa 56:9</reference> is both synonymous and progressive. The writer seeks for rare forms, because he is about to depict a rare inversion of the proper state of things. חיתו (with the first syllable loosely closed) is the antiquated form of connection, which was admissible even with ביּער following (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.9.1-Isa.9.2">Isa 9:1-2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.21">2Sa 1:21</reference>). On אתיוּ (= אתוּ), see at <reference osisRef="Isa.21.12">Isa 21:12</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.21.14">Isa 21:14</reference>).
entries.b60b43a0327a23fef30849bdffefd7c14b7fc783: <reference osisRef="Isa.56.10-Isa.56.11">Isa 56:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13558" type="x-p"/> The prophet now proceeds with צפו (צפיו): the suffix refers to Israel, which was also the object to לאכל. <hi type="italic">“His watchmen are blind: they </hi>(<hi type="italic">are</hi>)<hi type="italic">all ignorant, they </hi>(<hi type="italic">are</hi>)<hi type="italic">all dumb dogs that cannot bark; raving, lying down, loving to slumber. And the dogs are mightily greedy, they know no satiety; and such are shepherds! They know no understanding; they have all turned to their own ways, every one for his own gain throughout his border.”</hi> The “watchmen” are the prophets here, as everywhere else (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.21.6">Isa 21:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.1">Hab 2:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.17">Jer 6:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.3.17">Eze 3:17</reference>). The prophet is like a watchman (<hi type="italic">tsōpheh</hi>) stationed upon his watch-tower (<hi type="italic">specula</hi>), whose duty it is, when he sees the sword come upon the land, to blow the <hi type="italic">shōphâr</hi>, and warn the people (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.1-Ezek.33.9">Eze 33:1-9</reference>). But just as Jeremiah speaks of bad prophets among the captives (Jer 29), and the book of Ezekiel is full of reproaches at the existing neglect of the office of watchman and shepherd; so does the prophet here complain that the watchmen of the nation are blind, in direct opposition to both their title and their calling; they are all without either knowledge or the capacity for knowledge (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.44.9">Isa 44:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.20">Isa 45:20</reference>). They ought to resemble watchful sheep-dogs (<reference osisRef="Job.30.1">Job 30:1</reference>), which bark when the flock is threatened; but they are dumb, and cannot bark (<hi type="italic">nâbhach</hi>, root <hi type="italic">nab</hi>), and leave the flock to all its danger. Instead of being “seers” (<hi type="italic">chōzı̄m</hi>), they are ravers (<hi type="italic">hōzı̄m</hi>; cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Isa 19:18</reference>, where we have a play upon החרס in ההרס). הזים, from הזה, to rave in sickness, <hi type="italic">n. act. hadhajan</hi> (which Kimchi compares to <hi type="italic">parlare</hi> <hi type="italic">in</hi> <hi type="italic">sônno</hi>); hence the Targum נימים, lxx ἐνυπνιαζόμενοι A φανταζόμενοι, S ὁραματισταί, Jer. <hi type="italic">videntes vana</hi>. The predicates which follow are attached to the leading word <hi type="italic">hōzı̄m</hi> (raving), if not precisely as adjectives, yet as more minutely descriptive. Instead of watching, praying, wrestling, to render themselves susceptible of visions of divine revelations for the good of their people, and to keep themselves in readiness to receive them, they are idle, loving comfortable ease, talkers in their sleep. And the dogs, viz., those prophets who resemble the worst of them (see at <reference osisRef="Isa.40.8">Isa 40:8</reference>), are נפשׁ עזּי, of violent, unrestrained soul, insatiable. Their soul lives and moves in the lowest parts of their nature; it is nothing but selfish avarice, self-indulgent greediness, violent restlessness of passion, that revolves perpetually around itself. With the words “and these are shepherds,” the range of the prophet’s vision is extended to the leaders of the nation generally; for when the prophet adds as an exclamation, “And such (<hi type="italic">hi</hi> = tales) are shepherds!” he applies the glaring contrast between calling and conduct to the holders of both offices, that of teacher and that of ruler alike.
